utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, I know from the remarks you made to Mr. Ostojic yesterday that you appreciate advocates who get on with it, and that's precisely what I propose to do this afternoon. Pandurevic in his grounds of appeal actively pursued four grounds. Today I will present brief - and I do mean brief - oral submissions in support of only three of them. For reasons that I will explain at the conclusion of these submissions, I will not advance any oral arguments in respect of the fourth, and I anticipate that the Prosecution will wish to respond with correspondent economy. The first ground of Pandurevic's appeal relates to his convictions under Counts 4 and 5 of the indictment for aiding and abetting murder, and he says, through me, that they are open to criticism on a number of levels: Procedural, legal, and evidential. In my submission, they are unsupportable in their present form, and the trial's record is such that the conviction cannot be reconstituted or rectified by this Appeals Chamber. His convictions under Counts 4 and 5 relate to the murder of ten prisoners who had been held at the infirmary of the Zvornik Brigade sometime on or after the 23rd of July, 1995, and thus about a week or so after the more central events in the indictment with which you are all concerned. Those men had been injured and originally came from Milici, and it is thus by that epithet they are generally known - the Milici prisoners or the ten Milici men. They had been treated at the hospital in the town of Zvornik but transferred to the infirmary of the Zvornik Brigade on or about the 20th July for security reasons. At that time, the Zvornik Brigade was taking numbers of prisoners who had been part of the 28th Division and was holding them in its detention facilities, awaiting for them to be transferred to the ICRC facility at Batkovici. On the morning of the 23rd of July, there was a flurry of correspondence between the Zvornik Brigade and the Drina Corps, its superior organ. At 8.00 in the morning, Vinko Pandurevic raised - not for the first time - his concerns about the numbers of prisoners being held by the Zvornik Brigade, including the wounded ones. He spoke to a Colonel Cerovic, a deputy commander of the Drina Corps, and asked about the possibility of their exchange or their transfer to Batkovici. At about 8.30 in the morning, half an hour later, the duty officer at the Zvornik Brigade received a call from Cerovic, telling him that Popovic would be there by 1700 and would say what needs to be done with the work we talked about. As a matter of fact, on that day, Popovic was apparently assigned a car for a journey from the headquarters of the Drina Corps to go to Zvornik. In his evidence, Pandurevic did not see Popovic that day and he did not remember receiving the message from the duty officer. At 10.00 that morning, an hour and a half after the message, both Pandurevic and Obrenovic were at a brigade meeting. PW-168 was to say in his evidence that the prisoners were taken away early in the morning. The Trial Chamber found by majority, Judge Kwon dissenting, that Pandurevic, firstly, had received the message at 8.30 or shortly thereafter and necessarily before Popovic arrived; and secondly, that the message would have alerted him to the likely fate of the prisoners, and therefore convicted him of aiding and abetting their murder by Popovic by omission, namely, his failure to exercise his legal duty to protect them, and that his failure to protect them substantially contributed to their murder and that he had the necessary mens rea. It is accepted that Pandurevic had a legal duty to protect the ten prisoners; however, he complains as follows. Firstly, he was convicted of a form of liability which wasn't pleaded against him in the indictment by reason of which he was prejudiced. Secondly, the Trial Chamber conducted a deficient analysis of the legal elements of the offence with which he was charged. In particular, the Trial Chamber did not discuss nor consider what evidence there was of specific direction. Such analysis of that question, as might now be possible from other findings, must necessarily lead to a conclusion that there is insufficient evidence to find it ever existed. Thirdly, the Trial Chamber's findings as to Pandurevic's knowledge and other matters are based on the drawing of inappropriate and overstretched inference. These matters are extensively litigated in the various appellate filings by both parties and will be touched upon obliquely in due course. However, one topic requires particular attention and that is the requirement that the aider and abettor must be proved to have specifically directed his actions to assist, encourage, or lend moral support to the crime, in this case murder. The Trial Chamber defined aiding and abetting at paragraph 1014 of its judgement as follows: "An aider and abettor carries out acts specifically directed to assist, encourage, or lend moral support to the perpetration of a certain specific crime which have a substantial effect on the perpetration of the crime. The requisite mental element of aiding and abetting is knowledge that the acts performed assist the performance of the specific crime by the principal perpetrator." It went on to say: "... that 'specific direction' was not always included as an element of the actus reus of aiding and abetting." One can have some sympathy with the Trial Chamber expressing the elements of aiding and abetting in that way. They drew it from what they believed to be an accurate statement of the law, the cases of Blagojevic and Jokic. On the 28th of February of this year, this Appeals Chamber gave judgement in the case of Momcilo Perisic. In that case, the Appeals Chamber thoroughly reviewed the Tribunal's whole jurisprudence in cases of aiding and abetting and made clear statements as to what, in fact, the law was. At paragraph 36, the Appeals Chamber, Judge Liu dissenting, considered that: "... specific direction remains an element of the actus reus of aiding and abetting liability ..." It went on further to say that it reaffirmed that: "... no conviction for aiding and abetting may be entered if the element of specific direction is not established beyond reasonable doubt, either explicitly or implicitly." At paragraph 38 it allowed for -- or it went on to say when aiding and abetting involves "acts geographically or otherwise proximate to, and thus not remote from, the crimes of the principal perpetrators." Specific direction need not be explicitly discussed because it may be demonstrated implicitly through discussion of other elements such as substantial contribution. But at paragraph 39 it said: "Where an accused aider and abettor is remote from the relevant crimes, evidence proving other elements of aiding and abetting may not be sufficient to prove specific direction. In such circumstances," the Appeals Chamber held "that explicit consideration of specific direction is required." Throughout the appellate phase, the Prosecution has repeatedly denied that specific direction was an element of aiding and abetting. In paragraph 76 of its reply brief -- its response brief, I'm sorry, it said: "In accordance with established case law, the Chamber correctly held that specific direction is not an essential ingredient of the actus reus of aiding and abetting ..." And at paragraph 77, rather stridently: "Pandurevic's arguments in this subground are confused, vague, and undeveloped, they should be dismissed. Pandurevic has not shown any cogent reason for the Appeals Chamber to depart from the established case law for either the actus reus or mens rea standards for aiding and abetting." And at paragraph 80, in relation to actus reus: "If specific direction has any meaning, it is no more than an expression of a causal link between the conduct and the crime, equating to the conduct having a substantial effect on the crime." On the contrary, the Defence for Pandurevic has argued throughout that whether it is considered to be part of the mens rea or actus reus of aiding and abetting, direction or purposefulness should be an essential element of this mode of liability. The Trial Chamber did not discuss specific direction in relation to these offences, understandably because it didn't regard it as being a requisite element of the offence. The dismissal by the Trial Chamber of specific direction as an essential element of aiding and abetting renders in itself the convictions against Pandurevic unsupportable. Moreover, the particular form of aiding and abetting that Pandurevic was convicted of in relation to the ten prisoners further complicates matters. This was no ordinary case of aiding and abetting; it is one that he allegedly perpetrated through omission.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down for the sake of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Conceptually, that is a very complex and difficult notion. One is entitled to ask: How can you specifically direct an omission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, have you seen the request to slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. I'll go back. Conceptually, that is a very complicated and difficult notion. How can one specifically direct an omission in support of a third party? Even if you can conceive it, there's no recognised process for its legal construction. Firstly, there is no detailed discussion in ICTY jurisprudence on how to ascertain specific direction in aiding and abetting by omission, although the Appeals Chamber in Oric required aiding and abetting by omission to be directed to assist, encourage, or lend moral support to the perpetration of a crime and have a substantial effect upon the perpetration of a crime. In other words, any finding that Pandurevic is responsible for the murder of the ten military prisoners by aiding and abetting by omission should be based on ascertaining that such an omission was specifically directed at assisting, encouraging, or lending moral support to their murder. Neither is there any analogous help to be found in domestic case law. Secondly, as clarified in the Perisic case, when an accused aider and abettor is remote from relevant crimes, evidence proving other elements of aiding and abetting may not be sufficient to prove specific direction. In such circumstances, explicit consideration of specific direction is required. "Remote" was clarified as meaning geographically remote from the scene of the crime, in this case the murder of the ten men. Pandurevic was not a bystander on any version of events. The prisoners were taken away and murdered elsewhere. There is scant evidence as to either when or where that took place. In all senses of the word, he was remote from the commission of the offence he was said to have assisted. The logic of the Appeals Chamber's judgement in Perisic can perhaps be illustrated by a simple example, and I'm conscious of the fact that I may get into discussions of tacit approval and legal duty, but I'll give the example anyway. If a man stands guard by a door while somebody is beaten to death inside the room, then you can reasonably infer, without too much discussion of the matter, that not only does he know that his acts make a substantial contribution to the murder, but that he intends to assist or specifically directs his acts to the murder. If, however, that man were a guard and he left his post, permitting somebody to enter the room, but in leaving his post went a significant distance away, there would have to be some discussion as to whether there was evidence that he had done so with a view to assisting the murder. That is more parallel to the situation of Pandurevic, and we say that the absence of a discussion and a finding about specific direction of his acts to assist in murder had to be carried out and the absence of that invalidates his conviction. Moreover, the findings in the evidence even if reviewed now at the appellate phase would not support any establishment of specific direction on the part of Pandurevic, indeed quite the contrary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, you appear to be using the term "specific direction" in two senses. At one point you asked the question: How can one specifically direct an omission? And I understand that to mean -- "direct" there to mean "require" or "order" an omission. Then later on you speak of ascertaining that an omission was specifically directed at assisting, encouraging, or supporting the murder. In that sense, the term "direct" I understand to mean "aimed at." And in my view, that indeed is the correct understanding of the term "direct." It shouldn't be used to mean "ordering." And the case law doesn't support that. So speaking for myself, I have a difficulty with the term "specific direction" itself, because as used and certainly as it has come to be understood by the public, I think it is quite, quite misleading. The law, as I understand it, doesn't require you to show that a particular order was given by the aider and abettor that assisted in the commission of the crime. What it requires is that there be evidence that shows that the acts of the aider and abettor were specifically aimed at assisting, encouraging, and supporting the principal offence. So I picked up on it because I had intended to raise this with both yourself and the Prosecutor, and I'd like you to pay some attention to it. Of course, what I have said doesn't mean that you can't have evidence of an order, and if you have evidence of an order from the aider and abettor that would be the best, that would be the best evidence. But it is wrong to say that the law requires that there be evidence of an order. If the order is there and you have evidence of that, that's one item of evidence which, among others, could substantiate the aiding and abetting. But I do find that the term as it has been used, as I have said, is quite misleading. I mean, if one wanted to have a shorthand term, an abbreviated term, it seems to me it should have been expressed in the passive voice, acts which were specifically directed at. But the way it is formulated encourages an interpretation that you need to have evidence of an order. And I'm quite satisfied - unless you can persuade me otherwise - that that is not a legal requirement. And I raise it because I've seen articles written by eminent persons which address the issue in this way, that some order is required and that is not the law at all. As I said, the order may be one item of evidence but it shouldn't be translated into a criterion for specific directions. And so I fault the abbreviated term "specific direction."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can I say this, the word "direct" in English has that natural ambiguity because it can mean "to channel" or "aim." It can also mean "to order." It has been no part of my submission that there needs to be evidence of an order by the aider and abettor. It is my submission that the requirement for what has been termed "specific direction" is additional to the requirement for the act to be shown substantially to contribute and is additional to the base-level mens rea for aiding and abetting. I may already have indicated that there is a term of art which in my view is more helpful which distinguishes, for example, between the requisite contribution to being part of a JCE and the requisite for being an aider and abettor, and that is that the former requires you to intend to commit, whereas the latter requires you to intend to assist. But that is more than just knowing that your acts do assist. You have to intend in making your substantial contribution to assist, and that is what I believe is meant by the phrase "specific direction." But I'm entirely with Your Honour on this. I think it's an inelegant phrase. It's not helpful, and it has a necessary ambiguity at its heart which derives from the English word "direct." But I did not intend to submit to this Court that there is a requirement for an order. I intended to submit to that Court that there was a requirement for, as it were, an intention to assist expressed as a specific direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I was just briefly about to review the surrounding factual findings made by the Trial Chamber. They found, at paragraph 1898, that Pandurevic had put in place within the Zvornik Brigade a regime designed to guarantee the safety and security of all prisoners taken by the brigade at that time. They found, moreover, that he had instigated a system to safe-guard the security of the very injured prisoners we are concerned with in the Zvornik Brigade medical centre, at paragraph 1899. They found that he repeatedly requested the transfer of all prisoners to a transfer centre overseen by the ICRC at Batkovici. And they found that Pandurevic intended that prisoners should be exchanged or taken to Batkovici. Judge Kwon in his dissenting judgement points to the actual transfer of two wounded prisoners being held at about the same time to Batkovici as being highly relevant to the question of Pandurevic's understanding of what he believed Popovic might do. That would equally negate, I submit, any possible finding that Pandurevic's omission was specifically directed or intended to assist their murder. The Chamber's findings are, therefore, incapable of supporting a finding that Pandurevic's alleged omission in relation to the prisoners was specifically directed to assist or encourage their murder, irrespective of whether it was a substantial contribution to it. The finding that he possessed the necessary mens rea for aiding and abetting is equally palpably insufficient, as that indicates a mere knowledge that his acts assisted. Now, that is the only substantial submission I'm going to advance in relation to ground 1 of Pandurevic's appeal because the remaining grounds are so copiously litigated in the written filings and there's nothing I wish usefully to add to them. I don't abandon them, but for economy of time, I'll leave you to consider them in the filings. I do, however, go slightly off piste at this moment, and out of curiosity invite you to consider Judge Prost's remarks on persecution. The Chamber considered whether it would find Pandurevic further guilty of the offence of persecution. Judge Kwon, having declined to find him guilty of any offence at all, did not express an opinion on this topic. In Judge Prost's opinion, it is apparent that Judge Agius would have found the discriminatory element of that offence proved. But Judge Prost issued what I submit to you is a pragmatic, eloquent, and correct opinion as to the approach to be taken as to whether that discriminatory element can be proved. She submitted - and I adopt - that substantial contribution must be to the crime as a whole for which the accused is to be convicted. At the heart of the crime of persecution is the discriminatory nature of the act and the specific intent with which it is committed. It is not sufficient that Pandurevic through his omission made a substantial contribution to the crime of murder, knowing that the crime would probably be committed with discriminatory intent; rather, his contribution must be similarly discriminatory in nature. She found that Pandurevic had no discriminatory intent, he had no involvement in the circumstances which led to him having custody of the ten prisoners, they were brought to the Standard barracks on the orders of others, and Pandurevic neither arranged for their selection nor for their presence there. He placed them in harm's way and thereby substantially contributed to their murder. However, that omission in no way contributed to the crime of persecution, and she opined that such conviction would render the discriminatory component of that offence utterly meaningless. These may well be submissions for a future day, but I put them on the record now. In other words, what Judge Prost was saying - and I submit correctly so - it is a pointless exercise to enter a conviction for the aggravated form of the offence, where the accused's acts or omission and mens rea would be precisely the same for both offences. There must be some personal indicator of aggravation of the simple offence. As a matter of legal logic, I'm going to move from ground 1 to ground 3, and then come back to ground 2, because ground 3 is again a finding that Pandurevic aided and abetted a crime, though on this occasion it is the forcible transfer and persecution of those transferred out of Srebrenica. In the submission of the appellant, this conviction too suffers from the same fatal flaw as the convictions complained of in ground 1; namely, that the Chamber failed to apply the correct legal standard by failing to recognise that an aider and abettor's actions need to be specifically directed to the offence of the perpetrator, in this case forcible transfer and persecution. There is, moreover, we submit, no consequent analysis of the element of specific direction and no findings in that regard. Furthermore, any analysis of the Trial Chamber's findings necessarily leads to the conclusion that the Prosecution would have failed to prove to the required standard that Pandurevic had acted with the appropriate specific direction had that exercise been carried out by the Chamber or, indeed, even if it were appropriate were this Chamber to carry it out now. Lastly, the appellant submits that the conviction for persecution too must fall, as it depends upon the conviction for aiding and abetting forcible transfer. In our appeal findings we have advanced two arguments. Firstly, that the Trial Chamber has failed to consider whether Pandurevic specifically directed his actions towards assisting forcible transfer; and secondly, that the Trial Chamber erred when it found that he made a substantial contribution to the forcible transfer. In relation to the first of these arguments, we point out that it is unreasonable to accept that the military purpose of Krivaja 95 was lawful, but on the basis of his actions Pandurevic furthered the unlawful purpose of assisting in the forcible transfer. And in relation to the second, we point out that the Trial Chamber has made contradictory findings regarding Pandurevic's involvement, on the one hand saying that it was substantial and, on the other, when considering his liability for sentence, that it was limited. The Trial Chamber in its judgement found that there was no doubt that the attack was directed against the civilian population; however, it acknowledged the dual purpose of the attack. The Prosecution alleged that the forcible transfer was committed in three ways. Firstly, the forced bussing of the women and children from Potocari; secondly, the forced flight of the column of men; and thirdly, the forced bussing of the men separated at Potocari. The Trial Chamber found that the plan to evacuate the civilian population was in place before the forces had entered the town, and the Chamber found that the military component of the column had choices other than flight, they could have stayed and fought. That does not apply, however, to the civilian component. The Chamber did not find that the men separated out at Potocari had been forcibly transferred. The Trial Chamber was satisfied that the forcible transfer was carried out with discriminatory intent and again restated the law relating to aiding and abetting and highlighting that the aider and abettor needed to know the elements of the crimes which his acts were said to assist and know the principal has the specific intent where such a crime is alleged. The Trial Chamber found that Pandurevic knew of the plan to forcibly remove the Bosnian Muslim population from Srebrenica, and they assessed his intention from his actions and concluded that he lacked the intent to carry out the common purpose of the joint criminal enterprise. Indeed, it found that he carried out his orders and undertook the actions described with the intent to achieve the military objective of defeating the ABiH 28th Division forces in both enclaves; and further, that the disabling of the OPs, while illegal, could be considered to have been reasonably necessary for the legitimate aim of the operation. The Trial Chamber further noted that the majority of Pandurevic's military activities pursuant to the Krivaja 95 operation occurred prior to Karadzic's order for the VRS town -- for the VRS forces to take the town of Srebrenica. They went on to find that no other acts existed from which his intent could be inferred. No evidence existed that his forces were involved in targeting civilians. They noted that he was not involved in the actual transfer of civilians from Potocari, and there was no evidence that his troops were involved. Although, Your Honour, a lack of intent to forcibly transfer is not synonymous with an absence of specific direction in his actions to forcibly transfer, the nuance, as we have already discussed, is subtle. In simple language, the JCE member must have the intent to commit; the aider and abettor the intent to assist, though with the knowledge of the elements of the crime of the principal perpetrator. Again, I submit that the finding at paragraph 2010 that Pandurevic had the requisite mens rea for aiding and abetting is not a sufficient finding to satisfy the requirement, as we now know it to be, that there be a discussion and a finding in relation to his specific direction of his actions. The Trial Chamber did not consider specific direction, but given its findings as to his intention as evidenced by his actions, had it gone on to consider specific direction, it must necessarily have found it absent. Given that the basis for the conviction for persecution is forcible transfer, we submit that that must fall too. Nonetheless, in relation to that, I would simply remind you again of the submissions I made in relation to the observations of Judge Prost. Exactly the same observations would apply here in relation to the aggravated or greater offence. Now, that is the conclusion of my submissions in relation to the two aiding and abetting charges. I wonder whether that's not a good moment to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Under ground 2 of his Notice of Appeal, the Appellant Pandurevic contests the Trial Chamber's finding that he had effective control of the elements of the Zvornik Brigade who aided and abetted the murder operation during the critical period of about 30 to 40 hours after he returned to Zvornik on the 15th of July, up until the conclusion of the murders in the Zvornik municipality on the 17th of July. His arguments under this ground fall into two sections: Firstly, that he didn't have effective control of the Zvornik Brigade as an institution between the 4th and the 15th of July; and second, that after he returned to Zvornik on the 15th of July and learned of the murders, he did not take effective control of the elements of the Zvornik Brigade which were under the orders of the security officers tasked with murdering prisoners pursuant to Mladic's order. The finding that Vinko Pandurevic had effective control of the Zvornik Brigade between the 4th and 15th of July was, of course, only that of the majority, Judge Kwon again dissenting. Judge Kwon's primary objection was on the grounds that it offended the principle of singleness or unity of command, namely, that a military unit cannot have two commanders at the same time, which is, of course, precisely what the Trial Chamber did find. He also highlighted two strands of findings by the Trial Chamber which he felt were inconsistent with a finding that Pandurevic was in effective control of the Zvornik Brigade during that period. Firstly, that during that period Pandurevic was the commander of another and separate military unit, namely, Tactical Group 1 under the Krivaja 95 operation. The wider consideration of his actions and whereabouts during that period occurs at paragraphs 1842 to 1859 of the trial judgement. So that you can have, as it were, a graphic illustration of Pandurevic's movements and gain some idea of, as it were, his geographic remoteness from the brigade at that time, we're going to show you a short video that was shown to the Trial Chamber, it is 7D1059.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your Honours will doubtless recognise Srebrenica in the middle of the map, Bratunac where the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade were just to the north of Srebrenica. Then if one goes to the very top of the map, Karakaj above Zvornik is the location of the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade. And you will remember that in the maps that the Prosecution were showing you, all the action, as it were, by the 13th of July was taking place well to the north of that. The finishing position just below Podzeplje is where Pandurevic was with his units on the 14th of July, having made his way after Krivaja 95 over to the west and then down south towards Zepa. So that gives you some idea of what his movements are there prosaically described in the Trial Chamber's judgements after paragraph 1842. Unless you've got any questions about that map or that video, we can take that off the screen now. Judge Kwon noted that whilst Pandurevic remained the commander of Tactical Group 1, he couldn't return to Zvornik to resume command of the Zvornik Brigade without an express order from his commander, Krstic, and indeed that is what happened on the 15th of July. He also observes that Obrenovic's assumption of command during that time and his acceptance of orders from the corps command and his consequent giving of orders to others was inconsistent with Pandurevic having effective control or command of the brigade. Notwithstanding that, the majority found, that's paragraph 2027, that Pandurevic was throughout the period of the 4th to the 15th of July the commander in name and substance, and they went on to consider that he had effective control of the brigade. In this appeal, Pandurevic agrees with Judge Kwon's concerns and adopts them as submissions herein - thank you most kindly - but he would, with respect, add two further concerns which undermine the Trial Chamber's findings, and they are the following: Firstly, that Pandurevic on all the evidence was receiving no reports from the brigade about its activities; but secondly, perhaps most significantly of all given the heavy reliance placed upon it by the majority, the evidence of PW-168, who was clear that Pandurevic was not in command of the units which were commanded by Obrenovic. And one has to observe, if anybody would know that, PW-168 would. That finding is particularly poignant because it was, at least according to the normal theory of command structure, individuals and units from that set of people for which Pandurevic was found to bear responsibility by the Trial Chamber after the 15th of July, namely, those which Obrenovic commanded. Therefore, as a matter of logic, if Pandurevic did not command the units under Obrenovic's control between the 4th and the 15th of July, he would have to take command back upon his return. The majority's finding, therefore, that Pandurevic had effective control throughout the period is illogical, contrary to all the evidence on the topic, and one which no reasonable Trial Chamber could make. Having said that, there is a curiosity of language in the judgement. Having found at paragraph 2027 that Pandurevic was the commander of the Zvornik Brigade from the period to the 4th to the 15th of July in name and substance, it went on to consider what happened on the 15th of July, and this is discussed at paragraph 2031. Paragraph 2031 reads as follows, and this is a finding doubtless of the majority: "It was open to Pandurevic to re-take command at any point as he so clearly did upon his return on the 15th of July ..." One is bound to ask if the majority were of the view that Pandurevic's command was unbroken throughout the period of July, including both periods of the 4th to the 15th and thereafter, what it was he was able to re-take in their view on the 15th when he returned. By the time of Pandurevic's return on the 15th of July - and I'm moving on to consider the second period, and thus the second and third grounds or subgrounds of the appeal - by the time of Pandurevic's return, Obrenovic had effectively lost control of the brigade. As you will have noted in argument this morning, he had spent the whole of the 14th of July until about 11.00 a.m. on the 15th of July away from the brigade command, during which time substantially all of the prisoners had been brought into the area as well as the resources that had been brought along by Beara and Popovic from Bratunac and elsewhere. Obrenovic's absence through the 14th and early part of the 15th of July is relevant to his own knowledge, and thus what he could convey to Pandurevic upon his return. The infamous statement which you will doubtless hear a lot of in due course made by Obrenovic in the corridor of the Standard barracks upon Pandurevic's return is heavily indicative of his own bewilderment and impotence, though perhaps not as graphically illustrative of the situation in the Zvornik Brigade at that time, as the exclamation of Dragan Jokic, the Zvornik Brigade duty officer, earlier that morning that Beara and Popovic were taking whomever they wanted wherever they wanted. And you'll find that at paragraph 1861, footnote 5576. However, Obrenovic hadn't lost control of the whole brigade, just small elements of it for a day or two, a squad here, a driver there, perhaps a machinist. I want to pause now and simply make a graphic observation about how we submit command goes down or up through the ranks of an army. People often talk about a chain of command. In our submission, that's misleading. There are, in fact, several chains which run from the brigade commander. They run to his deputies and they run to his battalions. In the case of the Zvornik Brigade, there were eight battalions, thus eight chains. And within each battalion, there were a number of platoons and separate chains ran from the battalion command to them, and from them down to the men on the front to the men that drove the lorries to the men who tended the farms, which we heard about, to the men who dug the trenches. It is our submission and it is our case and always has been our case that those chains had links broken, links broken very often at the lowest level, and they were broken by Beara and Popovic and they were broken with the authority of Mladic, the supreme commander of the VRS. And those breaks in the chain here and there for a day or two, for a small element here, for a driver there, removed Vinko Pandurevic's -- or should I say firstly Dragan Obrenovic's and then Vinko Pandurevic's material ability effectively to control those elements of the Zvornik Brigade who were tasked with jobs by Beara and Popovic to do with the guarding or burying of prisoners. I'm going to take squarely on the chin the fact that Pandurevic did advance many of the arguments I'm about to mention to you at trial. However, if you look at the grounds and the brief on appeal, the complaint Pandurevic makes as to the Trial Chamber's judgement as to his ability to exercise effective control over the brigade on the 15th of July is not that they got it wrong, it is that they barely considered his case at all. Beara and Popovic did give orders to Zvornik Brigade soldiers, as the Trial Chamber found at paragraphs 1111, 1118 to 1120, 1122, 1132, 1134, 1278. Although the Prosecution in its response seeks to recharacterise those orders as requests or directions, that's what they were. Like Obrenovic, the units which Pandurevic lacked effective control over were small and disparate. Literally more than 99 per cent of the brigade's resources were under Pandurevic's command. They were at their combat units closer to their battalion commanders. They were fighting the column for at least a few hours until they were tasked by Pandurevic to assist Bosnian soldiers to pass through the corridor he had opened for them. But in relation to the whole brigade there were factors which bore upon Pandurevic's ability to exercise effective control adversely. As the Trial Chamber correctly observed at paragraph 2023, the test of effective control is whether the individual had the material ability to prevent or punish the perpetrators of crimes. It went on to find that the relevant factors to consider in determining material ability included the physical location of a superior, his responsibilities at the time, the information flow, and communication facilities with subordinates. We submit that all of the following were directly relevant to those considerations which, despite having identified, the Trial Chamber did not go on to consider. Firstly, there was a very limited period of time between Pandurevic's return to Zvornik and the conclusion of the killings. Secondly, the paucity of the information available to him. As you'll hear in due course, it amounted to no more than a three- or four-line conversation with Obrenovic who had been absent from the brigade for most of the previous day. The size of the brigade and its geographical spread. The Zvornik Brigade was a unit of uncommon size. It was 5.000 men strong and its units were spread across, quite literally, hundreds of square kilometres. Very few Zvornik Brigade soldiers were actually involved in assisting the operation. They're pretty well enumerated in our written filings. They were spread around the Zvornik municipality and critically they were not at their posts, self-evidently, and it is the Prosecution case, they were at schools and at fields or driving vehicles. They were not where they should have been and not acting according to the orders of their regular commanders. Accordingly, in this very small time-scale, they were neither easy to locate nor to bring under control. As you will know from the submissions you've already heard, from 1.00 on the 15th of July to 1.00 on the 16th of July, Pandurevic was completely engaged in a military situation. It was one in which his forces faced an attack from both sides and one in which he ultimately negotiated with the commander of the forces at Nezuk to let a column pass through and instructed his men to assist in that. There was no task in relation to the murder operation given to the Zvornik Brigade through the regular command chain, i.e., the Drina Corps. Such an order would have been recorded and thus capable of being followed down the chain. No, this operation was all done secretly. The prisoners themselves and their presence in the area created a difficulty for Pandurevic, as he was to say in a command report that day. And the presence of other forces in the Zvornik municipality, namely, units mixed together from Bratunac and elsewhere, mixed together by the perpetrators with Mladic's authority, in fact the majority of those involved in the killing operations in the Zvornik area had been brought from outside to conduct it. None of these arguments find voice in the Trial Chamber's judgement, and all of them would have been a relevant consideration to the factors which bear upon his ability effectively to exercise command. But perhaps I can graphically illustrate what I suggested to of many glaring omissions by way of material that we relied upon at trial. And I'm going to ask, please, if we can put on the screen P00417. Sorry, it's 7DP4117. These are the Provisional Service Regulations of the Army of the Serbian Republic, and they are one of the many documents control -- regulating the VRS at the time that were produced during the course of the trial. This document was produced by the Prosecution's military expert Richard Butler. It was interpreted through him. It was interpreted through, I think, at least two of the Defence military experts, and it was discussed with many, many of the senior command officers who gave evidence, both as part of the Prosecution and the Defence cases. I wonder now if we can go to page 10 in the English. I hope it's the same in the B/C/S. And can we focus in, please, on Article 16 and 17. Article 16 reads: "When several units are given a joint task, a commanding officer shall be appointed in good time to direct the execution of the task. If this is not regulated beforehand, the role of superior officer shall be assumed by the most senior officer who shall direct the execution of the task. "If a unit or an institution is suddenly left without a commanding officer, command shall be assumed by his deputy or the highest-ranking officer in that unit until a new commanding officer is appointed." Article 17 reads: "Members of the Army shall carry out the orders of their superiors without demur, in full, accurately and punctually. If by any chance the order was not given in good time, the person is required to take measures and act in accordance with the specific situation. "Members of the Army shall carry out the orders of the most senior officer present when the superior officer is absent. "The execution of each order shall first be reported to the superior officer or to the officer who has given the order." You won't be surprised to hear that the provisions of this document were a linchpin to Pandurevic's case at trial. You can see, I imagine, straight away how these provisions might relate to mixed units of soldiers under a commander from an outside institution. Let's be graphic about this. Beara or Popovic at a killing site in the Zvornik municipality with some Bratunac Brigade soldiers, some MUP units, some Skelani Brigade soldiers, and perhaps some people from the Zvornik Brigade, you can see how relevant it might have been and it was discussed extensively at trial. It was obliquely relied upon by the Trial Chamber as support for the proposition concerning the command of the Main Staff, and you'll find that at paragraph 106 of the judgement, footnote 254. But in relation to the command of the Zvornik Brigade, about which, of course, there was more controversy, it was simply disregarded. And you will find no reference to this provision in the text of the judgement or the footnotes under the discussion of the interruption of the command chain by the Trial Chamber. It wasn't discussed and reasoned away. It was just ignored. So, unhappily, was the evidence of a number of VRS and Zvornik Brigade officers who spoke about the exercise of command in the VRS generally. These included witnesses such as Dragutinovic, Galic, and Trivic, all called by the Prosecution. However, perhaps the most compelling example of all is that of Ostoja Stanisic, who was the commander of the 6th Battalion, called by the Prosecution. Given that this unit was involved in events at the Petkovci school and had direct contact with Beara, his evidence as to events on the ground and his perception as to who he was answerable are especially compelling. Amongst other things, this is what he said about the situation. And I'm going to invite the court officer, please, to put on the screen T 11705 from the 17th of May, 2007. It begins at line 6. He says: "As a battalion commander, I was responsible for my unit. If any higher officers from a higher command arrived, they could command me, they could take over the battalion, they could issue orders and I can only be their subordinate. "Q. Did you think what was going on at the time Petkovci school was under the control of somebody from higher command?" And he said: "As soon as the officers from the higher command came and we hadn't been informed about that, we had not received any orders from my command, I suppose that they had the supreme authority and that they held all the responsibility." No reference is made to this passage of evidence in the Trial Chamber's judgement. It is conspicuously absent from the section on command of the Zvornik Brigade during the killing operation. Again, it's not assessed and reasoned away, just ignored. Now, of course, army regulations as to ad hoc command structures in mixed or disrupted units are separate and distinct from legal considerations as to an accused's ability to exercise effective control. However, the interruption of a command chain, we submit, is quintessentially relevant. The killing operation was conducted by a wide variety of personnel from a number of military police and paramilitary units. The question of who was in command of the killing operation at each of the sites is one to which no answer has ever been given. Who told the drivers to drive? Who told the guards to guard? And who told the shooters to shoot? And who was in overall command at each site? The only possible answer to that on the Trial Chamber's findings is Beara and Popovic. There is almost no consideration of this central reality by the Trial Chamber and its impact upon the command of the Zvornik Brigade and the ability of Pandurevic and Obrenovic before him to exercise effective control of the elements taken by Beara and Popovic to aid and abet the killings. That failure to assess the reality of the situation and that ignorance of the crucial and central evidence is something that no reasonable Trial Chamber could or should have done. The Defence case was and remains that during the period from the 13th to the 17th of July, Beara and Popovic, with Mladic's authority, took and gave orders to disparate elements of the Zvornik Brigade in pursuit of their order to kill the prisoners. No reasonable Trial Chamber could have been satisfied so that it was sure that those few elements who were at the time under their orders were under the effective control of Vinko Pandurevic for the few hours between the 15th and the 17th of July. That concludes my submissions on ground 2 of Vinko Pandurevic's appeal. Ground 6, his appeal against sentence, will not be argued. It will not be argued because I abandoned the merits of his appeal, but it's simply pointless because no reduction in his sentence by this Chamber will have any practical impact. On the 23rd of November just passed, he had spent eight years and eight months in custody, and if you do the mathematics, you will realise that that is two-thirds of 13 years and he would, under the Tribunal's policy, be eligible for early release but for the fact of this appeal. We will in short order be submitting an application to the Appeals Chamber for provisional release, as we anticipate, given that this appeal has already taken three years to come to this stage, and the complexity and enormity of the appeals and cross-appeals you have to deal with, that its ultimate resolution is not about to happen in the near future. We would invite the Prosecution, rather than responding at length to an appeal against sentence that is not to be argued here today, rather to indicate what their attitude might be to an application for provisional release. I should make one submission, it is this: The appropriate starting point is that he has a sentence of 13 years' imprisonment. It is not open to either side, in my submission, to argue that it might go up or down in the future. Those are my submissions. Unless you have any questions, I will sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Yes, counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILANINIA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, Mr. President. May it please the Court. Your Honours, my name is Nema Milaninia, and on behalf of the Prosecution I will be addressing grounds 1 and 3 of the Defence's appeal. My colleague, Mr. Kyle Wood, will be addressing ground 2. Your Honours, like the Defence, we do not intend to make submissions on any other of the arguments that have not been addressed by oral submissions, and therefore rely upon our written submissions for those issues absent any questions from the Chamber. Your Honours, before I begin, I wish to make three observations. My first observation is that throughout their submissions the Defence has reflected a misunderstanding of the judgement. I note at appeal transcript 65 the Defence argued that on July 23rd Colonel Cerovic returned Pandurevic's phone call requesting a resolution to the issue concerning the prisoners at 8.30. That, Your Honours, is not true. As reflected at the judgement at paragraph 1904, as reflected in Exhibit P1310A, which is an intercept of that conversation between Colonel Cerovic and the duty officer, Colonel Cerovic returned Pandurevic's call only five minutes after and not 30. I raise this, Your Honours, as a matter because the Trial Chamber found that it was in light of the frequency of the events, that is, that Colonel Cerovic returned Pandurevic's calls only five minutes after, that it was left in part with no doubt that in light of its urgency, that Pandurevic was informed by the duty officer that Popovic would be coming later that day. I would also note, Your Honours, that the Defence misunderstands the Perisic appeals judgement. At appeals transcript 80, the Defence notes, and I state, that Pandurevic had the requisite mens rea for aiding and abetting is not a sufficient finding to satisfy the requirement as we know it to be. Your Honours, this conflation of purpose and specific direction is completely in opposite with the findings of the Perisic appeal judgement itself. And I quote paragraph 48 of the Perisic appeal judgement where the Chamber noted: "... the Appeals Chamber recalls again that the mens rea required to support a conviction for aiding and abetting is knowledge that assistance aids the commission of criminal acts, along with awareness of the essential elements of these crimes." Your Honours, I will go back to this issue again. And then finally, Your Honours, as a general observation, I note that the Defence alters its position today on appeal. The Defence argues, at appeals transcript page 69, that it has always been its position that specific direction is an actus reus requirement as well as a mens rea requirement. We note that this is in direct confliction with its own appeal brief, and I refer you to page 61 of their appeal brief where they argue that customary international law does not justify a mens rea standard without the assistance being purposely directed to the crimes. Your Honours, I highlight these matters for your attention only to explain why the -- why, through my submissions, I intend to reiterate the facts that are relevant at issue, but also to provide what we believe is an accurate reading of both the Perisic appeal judgement and its specific direction requirement. In that sense, Your Honours, I first turn to ground 3 to immediately dispose of the specific direction issue. As the Chamber will hear more tomorrow, between July 6th and July 11th, the VRS launched a co-ordinated and violent attack on the Srebrenica enclave, with the objective of forcibly removing the Bosnian Muslim population. This campaign comprised of ostensibly two phases. Between July 6 and July 9, the VRS subjected the enclave to daily mortar and artillery attacks and disabled UNPROFOR forces tasked with protecting the civilian population by removing them from their observation posts. After reducing the enclaves to their urban areas, the VRS began a take-over of Srebrenica town itself. On July 10th, the VRS launched rockets and artillery attacks into Srebrenica town, resulting in between 160 and 200 detonations. On July 11th, Srebrenica town, including the DutchBat compound, were subject to further shelling while the surrounding hills within which the town is located was secured. By the time, Your Honours, the Bosnian Serb forces descended from the hills into Srebrenica the afternoon of July 11th, the tens of thousands of Bosnian Muslims who had been in Srebrenica had been removed. As Your Honours know, Pandurevic, the appellant, is not remote to these events. He was an intimate participant in this campaign. He commanded a group of soldiers in these attacks and he was responsible for cleansing Srebrenica of Bosnian Muslims. The Chamber found that Pandurevic was responsible for removing DutchBat soldiers from their observation posts in the southern part of the enclave during the first phase of the attacks; that's judgement paragraph 1848. And after successfully removing UNPROFOR's presence, the Chamber found that Pandurevic participated in the take-over of Srebrenica itself by securing the surrounding hills before entering Srebrenica at 4.00 p.m. on July 11th; and that's the judgement paragraphs 1850 to 1851. Your Honours, the Chamber found that Pandurevic participated in these attacks, despite knowing that its very objective -- or that one of its objectives, excuse me, was to expel Bosnian Muslims out of the enclave and that his actions would facilitate that aim. That's judgement paragraphs 1994 and 2010. Notably, Your Honours, none of these findings are challenged by the Defence. Instead, the Defence raises two legal challenges -- I say "two" because its legal challenge in its brief was whether or not a purpose requirement should be established, and then it raises for the first time today its second legal challenge which is arguments on the basis of specific direction. Your Honours, I do not tend -- I will not explain why purpose is not a mens rea requirement for aiding and abetting. We have disposed of that issue in our appeal brief. And we would further note, in fact, that as I just referenced, the Perisic appeal judgement also disposed of that issue at paragraph 48 of its judgement. Therefore, I will go directly to their challenges concerning Perisic. Your Honours, whether or not this Chamber finds that Perisic should be overturned or whether or not this Chamber finds that the Trial Chamber rejected specific direction as a requirement in this case, the facts and the Chamber's findings show, without doubt, that there is -- that the specific direction test has been met on the findings that were made by the Trial Chamber. This is not a case like Perisic nor a case like the hypothetical posed by the Defence in their appeal and their reply brief, where there is a foreign military providing general assistance that could be used for either unlawful or lawful purposes. As I noted before, Pandurevic was not remote to the crimes. This is a case about a commander who was on the ground, participating in a campaign he knew to be unlawful, and committing acts he knew would facilitate that unlawful objective. In Perisic, Your Honours, the Appeals Chamber defined "specific direction" as: "... a culpable link between assistance provided by an accused ... and the crimes ..." That's Perisic appeals judgement 37. Importantly, Your Honours, I would note that the Defence completely failed to provide the Chamber the definition of "specific direction" in its articulation of what the test meant in the Perisic appeals judgement, but we would re-emphasise that in Perisic, the Appeals Chamber only defined "specific direction" as, I again quote, "a culpable link between the accused's acts of assistance and the crimes that were perpetrated." While the Prosecution believes that the contours of what that test and, specifically, what a culpable link consists of is vague and highly ambiguous, Perisic makes clear that at minimum specific direction can be demonstrated implicitly through the other elements of aiding and abetting, namely, substantial contribution and knowledge, where the aider and abettor's acts are geographically or otherwise proximate to the crimes of the principal perpetrators. That's Perisic paragraph 38. Your Honours, I emphasised "otherwise" because in the Defence's submissions they contended that Perisic only required that proximity exist geographically, as in an individual stood next to another individual committing the crimes. For instance, Your Honours, in Perisic, the Appeals Chamber found that Momcilo Perisic, the chief of the VJ, was remote from the crimes committed in the VRS because, one, the VRS was independent from the VJ; two, the VRS and the VJ were based in separate geographic regions; and three, that there was no evidence that Perisic himself was physically present when the relevant criminal acts were either planned or committed. And, Your Honours, that's Perisic paragraph 42. In this case, the evidence and the Chamber's findings demonstrate precisely the opposite. The culpable link between Pandurevic and the crimes is first evident by Pandurevic's proximity to the crimes. From July 5th until July 12th, Pandurevic was in or immediately around Srebrenica while commanding the 1st Tactical Group in the attack on the enclave and subsequently in the take-over of Srebrenica town itself. That's judgement paragraphs 1845 to 1855. Indeed, immediately after the Bosnian Muslims were expelled, Pandurevic's forces set up headquarters in Srebrenica town and Pandurevic himself was seen walking through the empty streets of Srebrenica with Mladic, Krstic, and Popovic. That's judgement paragraph 1851. Further, Your Honours, unlike in Perisic where the VJ and the VRS were in separate entities -- excuse me, were separate entities, the findings are abundantly clear that Pandurevic's 1st Tactical Group was a part and parcel of the very VRS forces that were engaged in the attacks on the enclaves. That's judgement paragraph 247. And finally, unlike in Perisic, Pandurevic was present during the briefing of Krivaja 95, when the unlawful objectives of the attacks were discussed at a command meeting on July 1st, at Pribicevac forward command post. He was also present in and around Srebrenica during virtually the entire time the town and the enclave were subject to the VRS's unlawful attack. That's judgement paragraphs 1842, 1846 to 1850. All together, Your Honours, we submit that these findings show, without a doubt, that Pandurevic -- that his -- Pandurevic's acts and assistance was proximate to the crimes of forcible transfer that were going on at the time. Indeed, Your Honours, he was certainly more proximate to the crimes than Krstic, who the Perisic Appeals Chamber found was a proximate aider and abettor at footnote 100 of its appeals judgement. During the relevant time, Krstic was located in Vlasenica or the forward command post in Zepa while his assets and his men were being used to commit or carry out the murder operation in Zvornik. That's Krstic Trial Chamber -- trial judgement, excuse me, paragraphs 378 and 413. In this case, Pandurevic was on the ground with his troops, engaged in the acts, assisting the forcible transfer campaign, and then subsequently, as you will hear on Monday or tomorrow, in Zvornik during the times in which his brigade members were carrying out or assisting the murder operation. Your Honours, the culpable link is also evident by Pandurevic's contributions to the forcible transfer campaign, a matter which the Defence touched upon today. The Chamber found that while Pandurevic's actions were part of the Krivaja 95 operation that included a legitimate military aim, his actions at the same time, simultaneously, supported the plan to forcibly remove the Bosnian Muslim population from Srebrenica. And that's judgement paragraph 1996. The Chamber found that in the Krivaja 95 order itself, that the 1st Tactical Group, which Pandurevic was responsible for commanding, had been specifically tasked with the purpose of reducing the enclave in addition to combatting the ABiH. That's judgement paragraph 247. In accordance with those objectives, the Chamber found that on July 8th, the 1st Tactical Group under Pandurevic's command unlawfully removed UNPROFOR soldiers from their observation posts located in the southern part of the enclave. And that's judgement paragraphs 770, 1997, and 2011. And as I noted before, Pandurevic's contributions also consisted of assisting the VRS in taking over Srebrenica town itself by securing the surrounding mountain range. And finally, Your Honours, the culpable link is evidenced in this case by the fact that Pandurevic himself knew that at the time in which he was participating in the attack, that his participation would assist the commission of the forcible transfer of the Bosnian Muslim population from the Srebrenica enclave. And that's judgement paragraph 2010. Pandurevic himself testified that in spring of 1995 he was aware of Zivanovic's 20 March 1995 order to the Drina Corps brigade commanders, which specifically reiterated the criminal objective of Directive 7, that through combat operations of the Bosnian Serb forces that they would, and I quote, "create an unbearable situation of total insecurity, with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." And that's judgement paragraph 1993 and transcript page 30822. Pandurevic in fact testified, Your Honours, that he believed Zivanovic's order to effectively take Directive 7 and adapt it to the Drina Corps's operations. That's transcript pages 31430 to 31431, which are cited also at footnote 555 of paragraph 201 of the judgement. In addition, Your Honours, Pandurevic also knew and implemented the two Krivaja 95 orders, which expressly refer to Directive 7 and 7/1 in outlining the tasks of the combat groups, including Pandurevic's combat unit. The second order of Krivaja 95, which was the combat order, specifically noted that one of the objectives of the attack was, and I quote, "to create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves." Judgement paragraph 1994. And then finally, Your Honours, I also note the interim combat report issued by Pandurevic on July 16th which is described at paragraph 1876 of the judgement and marked as Exhibit 7DP330. And, Your Honours, you can see an excerpt of that exhibit on your screens. As you can see, the last sentence of the report has been brought out in order to emphasise it, but it states very specifically in Pandurevic's own words, and I quote: "I consider the Krivaja 95 operation is not complete as long as a single enemy soldier or civilian remains behind the front line." Therefore, Your Honours, Pandurevic's own words left no doubt that he was aware that his orders involved expelling civilians from the enclaves. Together these facts and findings show that Pandurevic was proximate to the crimes, substantially contributed to them, and that he knew throughout the campaign that his acts would assist the commission of those crimes. The culpable link, therefore, between Pandurevic and the forcible transfer -- excuse me, forcible removal of the Bosnian Muslims is, therefore, met in this case. Your Honours, I therefore now turn to the events on July 23rd and also address the issue concerning specific direction, again emphasising why the culpable link between Pandurevic's acts of assistance and the crime of the murder were met on the facts of this case, regardless of whether or not this Chamber adopts Perisic as a valid articulation of the elements of aiding and abetting. Your Honours, I will not repeat our arguments on why the Chamber properly held that the mens rea required for aiding and abetting is knowledge. Instead, I will first explain -- excuse me, I will focus on explaining why that culpable link was met. First, the Chamber's findings make clear that Pandurevic was geographically or otherwise proximate to the crimes. The wounded prisoners were held in the custody of the Zvornik Brigade and guarded by the Zvornik Brigade military police, units commanded by Pandurevic himself, just like in the context of Krstic where his units and his assets were utilised in the -- in the commission of crimes in Zvornik. Further, the prisoners were detained at the medical unit in the Standard barracks in Karakaj, where Pandurevic himself was based throughout the relevant time. And Your Honours can find that at judgement paragraphs 1900, 1908, 1986, and transcript page 31159. Second, Pandurevic knew that it was probable that the wounded prisoners would be murdered once they were transferred into Popovic's custody. That's a finding that the judgement -- that the Trial Chamber made at paragraph 1898. During the trial, Your Honours, Pandurevic himself testified that by July 23rd he was fully aware that Popovic was in the Zvornik area and that Popovic had been involved in the execution of prisoners. That's judgement footnote 5730 and transcript pages 32261 to 32262. The evidence also showed that in his own conversations with Obrenovic on July 15th and July 17th, that Pandurevic learned of Popovic's key role in carrying out the murder of the Bosnian Muslim prisoners and that he had a full detail of not only the murder operation but of the details which you heard today on Monday concerning Popovic's significant role. And that, Your Honours, can be found at judgement paragraphs 1861 and 1883. And indeed, the evidence showed that sometime after the prisoners were taken away from Popovic and when asked about Obrenovic -- excuse me, when asked by Obrenovic about the wounded prisoners, Pandurevic himself replied that Popovic had arrived with an order from Mladic that the prisoners be "liquidated." That's judgement paragraph 1905. Finally, Your Honours, the culpable link is evidenced here in light of the direct link between Pandurevic's failure to act and the murder of the wounded prisoners. The Chamber found that Pandurevic had custody and control over the ten wounded prisoners who were detained at the Zvornik Brigade. That's judgement paragraph 1986. The Chamber also found that despite having the duty to take actions to protect the prisoners from being harmed when they were transferred to Popovic's custody that Pandurevic took no action whatsoever to prevent the custody of the prisoners from being transferred to Popovic. That's judgement paragraph 1988. In light of these facts and findings, Your Honours, there can be no doubt that there existed a culpable link between Pandurevic's acts -- excuse me, his omissions and the murder of the ten wounded patients in light of his proximity to the crimes, knowledge of Popovic's murderous propensity, and substantial contribution to the murders for his failure to exercise his legal duty to protect the prisoners. Your Honours, this concludes my submissions, but I would make one brief note. While we have argued that under the facts of this case, and especially in light of the Chamber's findings, that regardless of whether this Chamber adopts specific direction as a test as part of the jurisprudence of this Chamber, that we would note briefly the Prosecution's position -- excuse me, that -- if the Chamber were to accept specific direction that it would not alter the findings of this case. But putting that aside, we would note just briefly the Prosecution's position that specific direction is not an element of the actus reus of aiding and abetting, and that if the Court would like to hear detailed arguments to that effect, that we would be happy to provide supplemental submissions on that matter. Therefore, Your Honours, unless you have any questions, I would now pass the podium to my colleague Mr. Wood to address ground 2 of the Defence's appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll hear Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. As my colleague said, my name is Kyle Wood and I'll be handling the Prosecution's response to ground 2 to General Pandurevic's appeal. Let me start, Your Honours, by saying the only relevant issue in ground 2 is whether General Pandurevic, the Zvornik Brigade commander, had the material ability to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent his Zvornik Brigade subordinates from committing and aiding and abetting murders. The Chamber found that he did, and Pandurevic in his submissions and in his submissions here today fails to show that this finding was one that no reasonable finder of fact could reach. As you've heard, his attack takes two prongs. First, he challenges a finding that actually, Your Honours, has no bearing whatever on his conviction, that he had the material ability to prevent and punish his subordinates between the 4th of July and noon on the 15th of July. And this was when, as you've heard, General Pandurevic was busy attacking the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. Though the General himself admits that he could both communicate with and issue orders to his subordinates during this period, he nevertheless claims he was simply too busy to be able -- to have had the material ability to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent his subordinates or to punish their criminal acts. Second, as you've heard, General Pandurevic argues that he lacked the ability to prevent his front line soldiers, his military policemen, his engineers from perpetrating crimes between the 15th and the 17th of July, 1995, because they had been taken over by Mladic, Beara, and Popovic. Both of these arguments, Your Honours, are wrong in law and wrong in fact, and if accepted on these facts, they would stand for the proposition that a commander can avoid command responsibility by failing to exercise responsible command. So I'll turn then to Pandurevic's first argument which is also subject to Your Honours' first question. First -- again I note that the period between the 4th and the 15th of July has no bearing on the convictions that General Pandurevic actually appeals. But that said, I'll also note that General Pandurevic fails to show the Chamber's finding is one -- is unreasonable and that's because, first, it's consistent with Pandurevic's own admissions on this

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: three, as the Chamber pointed out, there was no order that replaced General Pandurevic as commander of the Zvornik Brigade in contrast to what happened when General Pandurevic was sent to the Krajina in August 1995 and Obrenovic was formally made acting commander of the Zvornik Brigade. Now, I start first with Pandurevic's admissions. The Trial Chamber found that Pandurevic admitted at trial that he retained formal command of the Zvornik Brigade and that he had the ability to both contact his brigade and to issue orders to his subordinates during the time that he was away attacking Srebrenica and Zepa. Rather, what they found is that he merely chose not to. This is at paragraph 2031 of the trial judgement. And in fact, Your Honours, an intercept shows that on the morning of the 15th of July, Pandurevic -- before Pandurevic had in fact returned to the Zvornik Brigade headquarters, he did order a subordinate to do a task and that that task was followed. He ordered his subordinate Miladin Mijatovic to "call the 4th, 6th, and 7th for me, check the conditions, and report back." This is all in footnote 5572 of the trial judgement, Your Honours. 15 minutes later, Mijatovic delivered the report his commander had ordered. Pandurevic essentially repeats this concession at paragraph 37 of his reply brief, when he admits that "he was not incapable of issuing one or more orders." The evidence shows that then, Your Honours, during his absence from the brigade from the 4th to noon on the 15th, he had the material ability to issue orders to his subordinates and that those orders were followed. Certainly, Your Honours, a commander who has the material ability to issue orders to his subordinates also has the material ability to prevent and punish them. Moving on then to Obrenovic, the Chamber also found that Obrenovic understood that Pandurevic remained the de facto commander of the Zvornik Brigade throughout 1995. Now, there are two instances in particular that illustrate this. First, the Chamber noted that PW-168 testified that Obrenovic had made a mistake when he neglected to notify Pandurevic that Obrenovic had granted the request of Drago Nikolic to participate in the murder operation and had ordered the military police to assist Nikolic. This is at trial judgement 2030. Now, why is this, Your Honours? It's because, according to this testimony, Obrenovic knew Nikolic was the direct subordinate of Pandurevic. That's at trial judgement 148. As such, he was required to keep his command informed of any requests for assistance from the security line. That's trial judgement 155. Obrenovic, as Chief of Staff, could only issue orders in the spirit of the commander's orders, and the commander had to be consulted on all taskings of the military police, the military police, Your Honours, which I will point out are also under (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And if we could briefly go into private session for this next portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Second, Your Honours, on the 15th of July, PW-168 testified that when Obrenovic concluded that the course of combat had reached a point at which he believed the military objective ought to change, that the column should be allowed to pass rather than militarily defeated, he required Pandurevic's approval. PW-168 testified that Obrenovic's first call was to the Drina Corps command to be connected with Pandurevic. And I know it's cumbersome, but if I could ask you to go back into private session just once more, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The evidence cited in paragraph 553 shows, Your Honours, that Obrenovic also understood that he -- Pandurevic remained in command and control of the Zvornik Brigade, otherwise Obrenovic himself would have just allowed the column to pass through the lines. And finally, Your Honours, as the Chamber noted, when General Pandurevic went to Srebrenica on the 4th of July, 1995, there was no order that replaced him as Zvornik Brigade commander on either a temporary or permanent basis. And the Chamber found this significant because it was in notable contrast to the situation a few weeks later in early August, when General Pandurevic was sent to the Krajina. In that situation, a formal order was issued, making Obrenovic the acting brigade commander. In his submissions, Your Honours, Pandurevic generally accepts many of these findings, but he argues in essence that he was merely too busy attacking Srebrenica and Zepa, on Krstic's orders, to be able to have the material ability to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent his subordinates' criminal acts and to punish them for those acts. Yet, he points to no evidence, either in his written submissions or here today, to show that the order sending him to participate in the attack on Srebrenica deprived him of the material ability to prevent and punish. Rather, what the evidence shows is that Pandurevic did not hesitate to continue to assert his authority with respect to the brigade when he chose to do so. That's at paragraph 2029. General Pandurevic argues here today, as he did in his brief, that somehow this finding about the irrelevant period infected the Chamber's findings about the only relevant period to his conviction, which is the period starting from noon on the 15th. Rather, Your Honours, the Chamber made distinct findings at paragraphs 2027 to 2031 about General Pandurevic's command and effective control throughout July. It then took up his argument about this period between the 4th and the 15th, it considered his argument, and it found that there was no evidence to support a finding that General Pandurevic had lost de facto control that he had maintained since he had assumed command of the Zvornik Brigade in December 1992. Rather, the Chamber relied on the evidence the Prosecution adduced, including Nikolic's request on the 13th of July that the regular command line was functioning in Pandurevic's absence. This brings us, Your Honour, to the second main challenge to the Chamber's finding.
